subject: Neurology
vignette: A 78-year-old woman reports gradual loss of central vision over several months. Funduscopy shows yellow subretinal deposits in the macula. There is no bleeding or distortion of straight lines.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Dry age-related macular degeneration
Wet age-related macular degeneration
Diabetic retinopathy
Retinitis pigmentosa
Central retinal artery occlusion

explanation_correct: Dry (atrophic) AMD is the most common form and causes gradual central vision loss due to degeneration of the macula with subretinal drusen deposits. Wet AMD is less common but causes more rapid vision loss from choroidal neovascularization with bleeding, and metamorphopsia (distortion of straight lines) is an early symptom. The gradual course, drusen, and absence of bleeding point to dry AMD.

explanation_incorrect.B: Wet AMD features choroidal neovascularization, bleeding, and metamorphopsia with more rapid vision loss, not just drusen.
explanation_incorrect.C: Diabetic retinopathy shows microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates in a diabetic patient.
explanation_incorrect.D: Retinitis pigmentosa causes night blindness, peripheral loss, bone spicules, and vessel attenuation, not macular drusen.
explanation_incorrect.E: Central retinal artery occlusion causes acute painless monocular vision loss with a cherry-red spot, not gradual central loss with drusen.

educationalObjective: Dry AMD is the most common type with gradual central vision loss and drusen; wet AMD adds neovascular bleeding and metamorphopsia.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 15 years has mild blurring of vision. Funduscopy shows microaneurysms, dot-and-blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates in both retinas. There is macular edema but no new vessel formation.
question: Which of the following best describes his retinopathy?

options.text: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy with vitreous hemorrhage
Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy with macular edema
Hypertensive retinopathy with a macular star
Retinal vein occlusion with a blood-and-thunder appearance
Age-related macular degeneration with drusen

explanation_correct: Chronic hyperglycemia increases retinal vascular permeability and causes occlusion, producing nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), the most common form, with microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates. Vision loss in NPDR is mainly due to macular edema. The absence of neovascularization distinguishes NPDR from proliferative disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Proliferative retinopathy is defined by retinal neovascularization that can cause vitreous hemorrhage and tractional detachment; none is present here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypertensive retinopathy shows arteriovenous nicking and copper wiring with a history of hypertension, not diabetes-associated microaneurysms.
explanation_incorrect.D: Retinal vein occlusion produces hemorrhage and venous engorgement in a venous distribution, not diffuse bilateral diabetic changes.
explanation_incorrect.E: AMD shows macular drusen or neovascular membranes, not microaneurysms and cotton-wool spots.

educationalObjective: NPDR shows microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates with vision loss from macular edema; PDR adds neovascularization.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing poorly controlled type 1 diabetes presents with sudden painless loss of vision in one eye. Examination shows vitreous hemorrhage. Funduscopy of the other eye shows friable new vessels on the retinal surface and optic disc.
question: Which of the following best explains the cause of her acute vision loss?

options.text: Rupture of a retinal macroaneurysm due to hypertension
Subretinal drusen deposition in the macula
Retinal neovascularization from chronic hypoxia causing vitreous hemorrhage
Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery
Acute angle-closure glaucoma

explanation_correct: In proliferative diabetic retinopathy, chronic retinal hypoxia drives neovascularization. These abnormal new vessels are fragile and can bleed into the vitreous, causing sudden painless vision loss, and can also produce tractional retinal detachment. This is distinct from NPDR, which lacks new vessels. Retinopathy of prematurity is another hypoxic neovascular retinal disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hypertensive macroaneurysm rupture is not the basis of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and no hypertension is described.
explanation_incorrect.B: Drusen are a feature of dry AMD, not diabetic neovascular disease.
explanation_incorrect.D: Retinal artery occlusion produces a cherry-red spot and acute painless loss from emboli, not vitreous hemorrhage from new vessels.
explanation_incorrect.E: Angle-closure glaucoma is a painful condition with a mid-dilated pupil, not painless vitreous hemorrhage.

educationalObjective: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy results from hypoxia-driven neovascularization that can cause vitreous hemorrhage and tractional detachment.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension has a blood pressure of 210/120 mm Hg. Funduscopy shows arteriovenous nicking, copper-wire arterioles, flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates forming a macular star. The optic discs are swollen.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of these findings?

options.text: Chronic hypertensive changes without urgency
Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy
Central retinal vein occlusion
Hypertensive retinopathy with papilledema indicating a hypertensive emergency
Optic neuritis

explanation_correct: Chronic hypertension causes spasm, sclerosis, and fibrinoid necrosis of retinal vessels, producing arteriovenous nicking, copper wiring, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates that may form a macular star. The presence of papilledema (bilateral disc swelling) indicates a hypertensive emergency and warrants immediate blood-pressure lowering.

explanation_incorrect.A: The presence of papilledema elevates this beyond chronic benign changes to a hypertensive emergency.
explanation_incorrect.B: Diabetic retinopathy features microaneurysms and is linked to hyperglycemia, not the AV nicking and copper wiring described.
explanation_incorrect.C: Retinal vein occlusion produces unilateral venous engorgement and blood-and-thunder hemorrhages, not bilateral chronic changes with papilledema.
explanation_incorrect.E: Optic neuritis causes acute painful monocular vision loss, not bilateral chronic hypertensive changes with a macular star.

educationalObjective: Hypertensive retinopathy shows AV nicking, copper wiring, and exudates; papilledema signifies a hypertensive emergency.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 68-year-old man experiences sudden painless loss of vision in his right eye. Funduscopy shows a cloudy, pale retina with a round cherry-red spot at the fovea. A small yellow refractile deposit is seen in a retinal arteriole.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause and diagnosis?

options.text: Central retinal vein occlusion from primary thrombosis
Branch retinal vein occlusion at an arteriovenous crossing
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Wet age-related macular degeneration
Retinal artery occlusion from an embolus, likely carotid in origin

explanation_correct: Retinal artery occlusion (central or branch) usually results from embolism, with carotid atherosclerosis more common than cardiogenic sources; giant cell arteritis is a less common cause. It produces acute painless monocular vision loss, a cloudy retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea, and visible emboli such as yellow refractile cholesterol crystals.

explanation_incorrect.A: Retinal vein occlusion produces retinal hemorrhage and venous engorgement (blood-and-thunder), not a cherry-red spot and emboli.
explanation_incorrect.B: Branch vein occlusion occurs at AV crossings with hemorrhages in a venous distribution, not arterial emboli and a pale retina.
explanation_incorrect.C: Retinal detachment presents with floaters, flashes, and a dark curtain with an elevated retina, not a cherry-red spot.
explanation_incorrect.D: Wet AMD causes central metamorphopsia and subretinal bleeding, not acute monocular loss with a cherry-red spot.

educationalObjective: Retinal artery occlusion causes acute painless monocular vision loss with a cherry-red spot and emboli, usually from carotid disease.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 64-year-old man with hypertension and atherosclerosis develops sudden visual loss in one eye. Funduscopy shows extensive retinal hemorrhage and dilated, tortuous veins giving a blood-and-thunder appearance in the distribution of a retinal vein.
question: Which of the following best describes the likely mechanism if this is a branch retinal vein occlusion?

options.text: Secondary thrombosis at an arteriovenous crossing where a sclerotic arteriole compresses the venule
Primary thrombosis of the central retinal vein within the optic nerve
Embolic occlusion by a cholesterol crystal from the carotid artery
Neovascularization from chronic retinal hypoxia
Autoimmune inflammation of the retinal veins

explanation_correct: Branch retinal vein occlusion is due to secondary thrombosis at arteriovenous crossings, where a sclerotic arteriole compresses the adjacent venule, causing turbulent flow and thrombosis. Central retinal vein occlusion, in contrast, is due to primary thrombosis. Both produce retinal hemorrhage and venous engorgement (blood and thunder) with retinal edema in affected areas.

explanation_incorrect.B: Primary thrombosis of the central retinal vein describes central, not branch, vein occlusion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cholesterol emboli occlude arteries, as in retinal artery occlusion, not venules at AV crossings.
explanation_incorrect.D: Neovascularization is a feature of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, not the primary event in vein occlusion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vein occlusion is thrombotic and compressive, not primarily an autoimmune vasculitis.

educationalObjective: Branch retinal vein occlusion results from thrombosis at AV crossings; central vein occlusion is a primary thrombosis; both cause a blood-and-thunder fundus.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 58-year-old man with high myopia reports seeing new floaters and flashes of light in his left eye, followed by a painless dark curtain descending across his vision over two days. Funduscopy shows an elevated, wrinkled retina with a change in vessel direction.
question: Which of the following best describes this condition and its management?

options.text: Exudative detachment from inflammation; treat with steroids
Central retinal artery occlusion; treat with thrombolytics
Vitreous hemorrhage from diabetes; observe conservatively
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, often with posterior vitreous detachment; surgical emergency
Dry age-related macular degeneration; monitor

explanation_correct: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the most common type and results from a retinal tear that allows vitreous fluid to separate the neurosensory retina from the pigment epithelium, interrupting choroidal blood supply. Risk factors include posterior vitreous detachment, advanced age, high myopia, and trauma. Symptoms include floaters and flashes followed by painless curtain-like vision loss, and it is a surgical emergency.

explanation_incorrect.A: Exudative (nonrhegmatogenous) detachment results from fluid accumulation due to inflammation or tumors, not the tears and PVD described.
explanation_incorrect.B: Retinal artery occlusion causes acute painless loss with a cherry-red spot, not an elevated wrinkled retina with a curtain.
explanation_incorrect.C: Vitreous hemorrhage from diabetes causes sudden vision loss but not an elevated detached retina with altered vessel direction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dry AMD causes gradual central loss with drusen, not a sudden curtain-like visual field defect.

educationalObjective: Rhegmatogenous detachment from a retinal tear (often with PVD or high myopia) causes floaters, flashes, and a dark curtain and is a surgical emergency.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 28-year-old man reports progressive difficulty seeing at night and loss of peripheral vision over several years. Funduscopy shows pallor of the optic disc, attenuation of retinal vessels, and black bone-spicule-shaped pigment deposits in the mid-periphery.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Retinopathy of prematurity
Hypertensive retinopathy
Retinitis pigmentosa
Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy
Central retinal vein occlusion

explanation_correct: Retinitis pigmentosa is a group of inherited dystrophies causing progressive degeneration of photoreceptors and the retinal pigment epithelium. Early symptoms are night blindness (nyctalopia) and peripheral vision loss, with a classic funduscopic triad of optic disc pallor, retinal vessel attenuation, and bone-spicule pigmentation. It may be associated with abetalipoproteinemia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Retinopathy of prematurity occurs in preterm infants exposed to hyperoxia with neovascularization, not a young adult with bone spicules.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hypertensive retinopathy shows AV nicking, copper wiring, and hemorrhages in a hypertensive patient, not night blindness and bone spicules.
explanation_incorrect.D: Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy shows microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates in a diabetic patient.
explanation_incorrect.E: Central retinal vein occlusion causes unilateral blood-and-thunder hemorrhage and venous engorgement, not a chronic inherited pigmentary dystrophy.

educationalObjective: Retinitis pigmentosa causes night blindness and peripheral loss with disc pallor, vessel attenuation, and bone-spicule pigmentation.
